client: I’ve been feeling really down since I failed my calculus final. I keep questioning whether I’m even cut out for my major or if I’m just fooling myself. I’m not sure if talking about it here will really change anything—I feel like I’m just not good enough, no matter what I do.
therapist: It sounds like failing that exam has really shaken your confidence and led to some harsh self-judgments. When you say "I’m not good enough, no matter what I do," I wonder if that thought feels true in other areas of your life too, or if it’s specific to this situation?

client: I think it's mostly about school, but maybe not just this class. Last semester I barely passed physics, and now with calculus...it's like I keep hitting walls in all my STEM classes. But when I'm with friends or doing other things, I don't feel this way as much. It's just academics that make me question everything.
therapist: It makes sense that you're feeling particularly discouraged about your STEM classes since you've had challenging experiences in both physics and calculus. I notice that this pattern doesn't seem to extend to other areas of your life like friendships, which suggests you might have different standards for yourself when it comes to academics. What do you think might be different about how you approach your STEM classes versus other areas where you feel more confident?

client: I guess with friends I don't have to be perfect. If I say something dumb or forget plans, it's not the end of the world. But with STEM classes, I feel like every point matters and one mistake means I'm not smart enough. My parents always talk about how important grades are for my future, so maybe that pressure makes it feel different. But I don't know how to turn that pressure off.
therapist: It sounds like there's a much higher standard for perfection in academics, especially with your parents' expectations weighing on you. That pressure to be perfect must make every mistake feel so much more significant than when you're with friends. Have you noticed any times when you were able to approach your STEM classes with more of that forgiving mindset you have with friends?

client: There was one lab in chemistry last month where I messed up the measurements, but my partner just laughed and said we'd redo it together. I didn't beat myself up as much that time. But that was different because it wasn't graded individually. When my own grade is on the line, that forgiving feeling disappears so fast. Like with this calculus final - it was all me, and I failed all by myself.
therapist: That chemistry lab moment shows you're capable of being kinder to yourself when you make mistakes, even in STEM—it's just harder when it feels like everything rides on your individual performance. I'm curious, what do you think might happen if you tried applying that same collaborative, forgiving mindset to your individual work?

client: I don't know...when it's individual work, it feels like being forgiving would just mean making excuses for being lazy. If I say "it's okay" about failing the calc final, won't that just make me slack off more? I worry I'll lose whatever small motivation I have left if I stop being hard on myself.
therapist: It's understandable to worry that self-compassion might lower your standards—that's a common fear. But what if being kinder to yourself could actually help you approach challenges with more energy and less fear? When you think about your calculus final, do you think being hard on yourself helped or hindered your preparation?

client: Honestly, I was so anxious before the final that I barely slept for two days. I kept telling myself I had to get an A to prove I wasn't a failure, and then I blanked during the test. I see what you mean about it not helping, but it's scary to try anything else - what if I stop caring completely?
therapist: It sounds like that intense pressure and self-criticism actually made it harder for you to perform at your best when it mattered most. That fear of stopping caring makes perfect sense—what if we explored a middle ground where you could care just as much, but in a way that supports rather than overwhelms you?

client: A middle ground sounds good in theory, but I don't know how to get there. Every time I try to be kinder to myself, that voice in my head says I'm just making excuses. How do I care without criticizing myself so harshly? It feels like I don't know any other way to motivate myself.
therapist: That critical voice has been your motivator for so long, so it's understandable that trying something new feels unfamiliar and even risky. Maybe we could experiment with shifting just one small self-critical thought at a time—what's one neutral or kind thing you could tell yourself after making a mistake, while still maintaining your commitment to doing well?

client: I could try saying something like "This is hard, but I'm doing my best" instead of "I'm such a failure." But part of me thinks that's just lying to myself—if I were really doing my best, wouldn't I have done better on the final? It's hard to believe that being kind will actually help me improve.
therapist: That's a really honest reflection—it makes sense that this new approach feels like it might not match your experience. What if we looked at your preparation for the final more objectively? You mentioned being sleep-deprived and extremely anxious—do those conditions sound like someone who was truly able to do their best work?

client: When you put it that way, I guess being exhausted and panicking wasn't my best state for taking a test. But I still feel like it's my fault for letting myself get that way—if I were stronger or smarter, I would have handled the pressure better. It's hard to separate the results from myself as a person.
therapist: It sounds like there's a deep belief here that your worth is tied to academic performance—that if you struggle, it means something fundamental about who you are. I wonder how you might respond if a close friend came to you describing this same experience? Would you judge them as harshly as you're judging yourself?

client: If a friend told me they failed a test, I'd probably tell them it's just one exam and doesn't define them. But with myself, it feels different—like my grades are proof of who I am. I know that's probably not fair, but it's hard to see myself the way I see others. Even if I tell myself it's just one test, that voice says "But what if you keep failing?"
therapist: It's powerful that you can recognize this double standard—that you offer friends compassion you struggle to give yourself. That fear of continued failure makes sense too, especially when so much feels at stake. What would it look like to bring even a small piece of that friend's perspective into how you talk to yourself after setbacks?
